CyberDefendersNetwork ForensicsEasyRetiredWireshark
Scenario: In September 2020 the SOC flagged suspicious activity from a user device, triggered by unusual SMB usage. Initial analysis pointed to a compromised privileged account and the use of a remote access tool. Three small PCAPs — Traffic-1, Traffic-2, and Traffic-3 — each cover a slice of the intrusion: authentication and log clearing, RPC over a named pipe, and remote execution.

Traffic-1.pcapng

Q1The attacker's activity showed extensive SMB protocol usage, indicating a potential pattern of significant data transfer or file access. What is the total number of bytes of the SMB protocol?
Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy. In the SMB row the Bytes column reads 4,406 (70.4% of the capture's 6,262 bytes). That figure includes the DCE/RPC payload nested underneath; the separate End Bytes column (3,765) counts only bytes not claimed by a child protocol.
answer4406
Q2Which username was utilized for authentication via SMB?
At only 32 packets it is quicker to read the capture than to filter it. Frame 27 is the SMB Session Setup Request carrying the NTLMSSP_AUTH message, and the Info column prints the account as User: \Administrator — a privileged account, confirming the SOC's suspicion. (ntlmssp.auth.username shows the same value.)
answerAdministrator
Q3What is the name of the file that was opened by the attacker?
After the Tree Connect to \\172.16.66.36\IPC$, frame 31 is an NT Create AndX Request for the path \eventlog. That "file" is actually the named pipe for the remote Event Log RPC service — the same service behind the OpenEventLogW and ClearEventLogW calls in frames 18–19.
answereventlog
Q4What is the timestamp of the attempt to clear the event log? (24-hour UTC format)
smb
Frame 19 is the EVENTLOG ClearEventLogW request, at 2020-09-23 16:50:16.73, immediately after OpenEventLogW in frame 18. Clearing logs is a classic defense-evasion step (T1070.001) — and the timestamp anchors the attacker timeline.
answer2020-09-23 16:50

Traffic-2.pcapng

Q5What is the name of the service that communicated using this named pipe?
frame contains 5c:00:50:00:49:00:50:00:45
SMB and DCE/RPC strings are UTF-16, so searching for the pipe prefix \PIPE means searching its UTF-16 bytes (5c 00 50 00 49 00 50 00 45). The hit is frame 25, a DCOM RemoteCreateInstance response; right-click → Follow → TCP Stream shows the endpoint binding [\PIPE\atsvc]. atsvc is the legacy Windows AT / Task Scheduler RPC interface, used to create scheduled tasks remotely — a lateral-movement red flag (T1053).
answeratsvc
Q6What was the duration of communication between the identified addresses 172.16.66.1 and 172.16.66.36?
Statistics → Conversations → IPv4. The 172.16.66.1 ↔ 172.16.66.36 row shows 133 packets / 104 kB with a Duration of 11.7247 seconds — a very short window for everything the attacker did.
answer11.7247

Traffic-3.pcapng

Q7Which username was used to set up these potentially suspicious requests?
Frame 5 is an SMB2 Session Setup Request (NTLMSSP_AUTH) from 172.16.66.1 to 172.16.66.36 whose Info column reads User: 3B\backdoor — a non-standard account name, followed straight away by a Tree Connect to \\172.16.66.36\ADMIN$.
answerbackdoor
Q8What is the name of the executable file utilized to execute processes remotely?
After the ADMIN$ connect, frame 11 is an SMB2 Create Request for PSEXESVC.exe, followed by large Write Requests (up to 65,536 bytes each) streaming the binary into the share, then a DCERPC Bind. That is PsExec's signature: drop the service binary on ADMIN$, then use RPC to install and start it. See the PsExec Hunt writeup for the full share-by-share walkthrough.
answerPSEXESVC.exe

Lessons learned: Small captures reward reading rather than filtering, but a few habits scale: in Protocol Hierarchy, know the difference between Bytes (including child protocols) and End Bytes; search SMB and RPC strings as UTF-16; and use Conversations for durations. Each stage is also a detection opportunity — remote ClearEventLogW calls over SMB (the target logs Security event 1102 / System event 104), atsvc pipe use between workstations, an unfamiliar account like backdoor authenticating over SMB, and PSEXESVC.exe landing on ADMIN$. Alert on the behavior, not just the tool name.
